Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National Sliding-scale mining royalties generate GH¢7.8bn for Ghana – Mahama Source : Maxwell Agbagba 17 November 2026 8:21pm President John Dramani Mahama ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
President John Mahama says Ghana has generated GH¢7.8 billion in royalties from large-scale gold mining companies since the introduction of a sliding-scale royalty regime this year, as part of efforts to ensure the country's mineral wealth benefits its people.
He says African countries must rethink existing mineral agreements and exercise more control over their natural resources to ensure that the wealth extracted translates into jobs, investment and improved living conditions for communities.
Speaking at the West Africa Integration and Investment Summit in Sierra Leone, President Mahama said Ghana had moved away from fixed royalty arrangements that locked payments at three per cent under development and stability agreements.
Under the new arrangement, royalties are adjusted according to prevailing gold prices, with the rate ranging from five per cent when prices are low to 12 per cent when they rise.
“So we signed the development agreements and locked in the royalty at 3%. So today I said, no, we cannot have that. Let us change to a sliding scale, so if the price comes down, we will come to the minimum royalty, 5%. If it goes up, as gold has done, we'll charge you 12%,” he said.
President Mahama disclosed that since the law was passed in 2026, large-scale gold mining companies had paid GH¢7.8 billion in royalties.
He said, “So since we passed that law, gold has remained high, so we are getting 12%. From when the law was passed this year, 7.8 billion Ghana cedis have been paid as royalties for big-scale gold. We must look at all these mineral rights again and see how we invest in order that it benefits our people”.
He argued that Africa must move beyond mineral extraction arrangements that create wealth elsewhere while leaving host communities in poverty.
“From our colonial inheritance, we were taught that people come and ask for concessions, we sign a concession, a 30-year concession, and where does the value go? It goes to build wealth in other jurisdictions,” he said.
President Mahama also cited Ghana's Gold Board as another measure aimed at retaining more value from the country's mineral resources.
He said artisanal and small-scale gold production increased from 64 tonnes, valued at $4.6 billion in 2024, to 104 tonnes, generating $10.8 billion for the Ghanaian economy following the introduction of the Gold Board law. The law requires all gold exports to pass through the Gold Board, with violations attracting confiscation of the gold and imprisonment.
President Mahama said the main objective was to ensure that Africa's natural resources become a source of wealth and prosperity for its people.
“African minerals must be a source of wealth and prosperity for African people,” he stressed.
